client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't bring myself to go, because being around everyone just makes her absence feel even more overwhelming. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: I'm really glad you decided to reach out, even through the uncertainty about whether it will help — that took courage, and it tells me a part of you is still looking for a way through this. Losing your grandmother and then facing those family gatherings without her sounds incredibly painful, like every reunion becomes a reminder of the empty space she's left behind. I'm curious — when you imagine being at one of those get-togethers, what does that overwhelming feeling feel like for you in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's like this heavy pressure in my chest, and I can't really breathe properly. Everyone's laughing and talking and I just keep thinking, "She should be here, she's supposed to be here," and it feels almost like a betrayal to be around all that noise when she's gone. I end up feeling guilty for even trying to have a good time, like I don't deserve to.
therapist: What you're describing — that chest pressure, the guilt about even trying to enjoy yourself — is such a painful place to be, and it makes a lot of sense given how much you loved her. I notice as you're sharing something that feels so heavy, there's something almost careful or contained in the way you're telling it, like you might be holding a lot more back than the words alone are carrying. I'm wondering — is it hard to let yourself fully feel the weight of this, even here in this space?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, yeah, it is hard. I feel like if I actually let myself go there fully, I won't be able to pull myself back together, and then what? I still have to go home and function, go to work, pretend everything's fine — I can't afford to just fall apart.
therapist: That fear of "falling apart and not coming back" is one of the most common things that keeps grief locked inside, and it makes complete sense that you've been holding it together so tightly — you've had to. I want to gently offer a different possibility though: what if allowing yourself to feel this, even in small doses, might actually make it *less* likely to overwhelm you over time, rather than more? What do you think it would mean for you if "falling apart" for a moment didn't actually mean you were broken?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but I'm not sure I trust it. Like, what does "small doses" even look like in practice? Because in my experience, once I start crying or really going there, it doesn't just stay small — it kind of takes over, and I don't have a lot of evidence that it gets better afterward.
therapist: That's a really honest and important pushback, and your skepticism makes sense — I shouldn't ask you to trust something that hasn't matched your experience yet. What you're describing, where it feels like once the floodgates open there's no off switch, is actually really common with grief that's been held tightly for a while. I'm curious, when you've cried or "gone there" in the past, what actually happened afterward — even if it felt awful, did you eventually come back to yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean, yeah, I guess I did eventually come back to myself, but it always felt exhausting and hollow afterward, not like some kind of relief. I'd just feel wrung out and then kind of embarrassed, like I'd made a mess of myself for nothing. So even if I technically "came back," it didn't feel like it helped.
therapist: That exhaustion and embarrassment afterward — feeling like you "made a mess for nothing" — actually tells me something important: you've been grieving without any real support around it, which means it *would* feel hollow, because you were carrying it alone and then judging yourself for it afterward. The relief people talk about doesn't usually come from the crying itself, but from feeling witnessed and not having to hold it so tightly on your own. I wonder if part of what we could work on together is changing that "aftermath" experience, so it feels less like a mess and more like something that makes sense given how much you've lost.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes some sense to me, the part about being alone with it — because I really haven't talked to anyone about this, not properly. My family's all grieving too and I don't want to burden them, and my friends didn't really know her so it feels weird to bring it up. But I guess I'm still not totally sure what "being witnessed" looks like, or whether I'd even let myself be witnessed without shutting down halfway through.
therapist: It sounds like you've been carrying this in a kind of isolation — not because people aren't there, but because every direction you look, it feels like there's a reason not to burden them, which means you've had nowhere to put it. And what you just said about not being sure you'd let yourself be witnessed without shutting down — I think that's actually a really important thing to name, because it suggests a part of you is already anticipating protecting yourself, even here. I'm wondering, what do you think that shutting down is trying to protect you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it's protecting me from being seen as someone who can't handle things, or who's too much for other people to deal with. Like, if I really let someone see how bad it's been, they might pull away or not know what to say, and then I'd feel even more alone than I do now. That almost seems worse than just keeping it to myself.
therapist: That fear — "if they really see me, they'll pull away, and I'll end up more alone" — is such a painful catch-22 to be stuck in, and it makes complete sense that keeping it to yourself has felt like the safer option. I notice there's something quite urgent in the way you're describing this, like this fear is very alive for you right now, not just a distant worry. I'm curious — has there ever been a moment, even a small one, where you let someone see a vulnerable part of you and they *didn't* pull away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: There was this one time, maybe a few years ago, where I broke down in front of a close friend after a really bad week, and she just sat with me and didn't try to fix anything or make it weird. But I keep telling myself that was different, that grief is heavier and messier than just having a bad week, and I'm not sure people can handle that the same way. So even though that happened, I'm not sure I can count on it happening again.
therapist: You actually have real evidence that being witnessed didn't lead to someone pulling away — your friend sat with you, didn't try to fix it, and didn't make it weird, and that's exactly what being witnessed can look like. I notice you're working quite hard to talk yourself out of counting that experience, almost like your mind is protecting you from hoping it could happen again. What do you think it would mean to let that memory be evidence that you *are* someone people can show up for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess it would mean that maybe I'm not as much of a burden as I think I am, which is... a strange thing to even consider. But there's this part of me that immediately wants to say, "Yeah, but that friend is different, she's just unusually good at that kind of thing," like I'm already finding a way to make it the exception rather than the rule. I don't know why I'm so determined to believe the worst version of how people would respond to me.
therapist: You just caught yourself in real time doing something really significant — watching your own mind dismiss the evidence before it can mean anything, and then actually wondering *why* you do that, which takes a lot of self-awareness. That question you ended with — "why am I so determined to believe the worst version?" — I think that might be one of the most important questions we could sit with together. Where do you think that determination came from — is it something you learned somewhere along the way, that believing the worst kept you safer somehow?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech

client: I think maybe it did keep me safer at some point, like if I never expected people to show up for me then I couldn't be disappointed when they didn't. Growing up, my family wasn't great at talking about feelings — everyone just kind of got on with things, and showing emotion felt like it made people uncomfortable. So I guess I learned pretty early that it was easier to just not need anything from anyone.
therapist: What you just described — learning as a child that your emotions made others uncomfortable, so you tucked them away to keep the peace — that's not a flaw in you, that was a really smart adaptation that helped you survive your environment at the time. I notice as you're sharing something so foundational, your voice carries a kind of quiet heaviness to it, like this is landing somewhere deep rather than just being an intellectual insight. I'm wondering how it feels to say that out loud — that you learned so early not to need anything from anyone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
